First listed 2025-06-23 · episode or wrap

Is Capitalism Flawed? Fixing and Regulating Free Markets

Eisman and John Cassidy discuss capitalism's critics, Keynesian demand management, monetary targeting, financial incentives and the case for regulated markets. Eisman's recurring emphasis is capital, incentives and factual revision, with an explicit uncertain view of tariff intent. Most historical and political judgments are not trading forecasts.

YouTube · 2025-06-23 ↗Substack · 2025-06-23 ↗
Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

youtube-r1uFaatp4v8-c010 · material factual premise

Lower profits would mean higher wages.

Wrong
Source · 18:53-18:59 ↗
SpeakerJohn Cassidy
Stanceasserted
Horizonnot stated
Materialitysupporting

This is not a general accounting implication. Revenue can fall or nonwage costs can rise while wages are unchanged; a falling rate of profit is also not the same as a falling profit share.

Conditional reasoning

Revenue 100, wages 50 and other costs 30 imply profit 20. Revenue falling to 90 with costs unchanged reduces profit to 10 without raising wages.

  • Profit equals revenue minus wages and other costs.
  • No fixed-output, fixed-other-cost assumption is supplied.

youtube-r1uFaatp4v8-c018 · explanation

GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports; if private spending and trade collapse, government is the only available source of recovery.

Mixed
Source · 27:50-28:44 ↗
SpeakerSteve Eisman
Stanceasserted
Horizonnot stated
Materialitymajor

The expenditure identity is correct, but it is an accounting decomposition rather than proof that private demand cannot recover or monetary and external adjustments cannot help. Falling gross trade does not necessarily mean falling net exports.

Conditional reasoning

Y=C+I+G+X-M. An increase in C, I or X-M can raise Y with G fixed. If exports fall from 100 to 80 and imports from 120 to 90, net exports improve from -20 to -10 despite both flows shrinking.

  • GDP is measured by final domestic expenditures plus exports minus imports.
  • Behavioral responses are not fixed by this identity.

Conditional reasoning

Government purchases create initial income; a marginal propensity to consume between zero and one generates further rounds. A positive activity effect does not establish positive net welfare after financing and opportunity costs.

  • Idle resources can be employed without displacing equally valuable private production.
  • Recipients spend some incremental income and financing does not fully offset demand.

  • The old correlation depended on behavior that was not invariant to policy.

Right
Source · 49:30-50:14 ↗
SpeakerSteve Eisman
Stanceasserted
Horizonnot stated
Materialitymajor

The conditional relationship follows from the explicit assumptions; it does not establish that those assumptions hold in observed markets.

Conditional reasoning

At 40 times assets/equity, a 2.5% asset loss consumes equity. At 12 times, equity covers about 8.33% of assets. Lower leverage increases this arithmetic loss buffer, without ensuring liquidity or eliminating concentration risk.

  • Asset values fall by the same fraction at otherwise comparable institutions.
  • Losses first reduce common equity, with no offsetting profits or hedges.

How he reasons here

  • Revise theories when contrary facts persist.
  • Separate privately profitable incentives from system-wide outcomes.
  • Evaluate bank gross leverage and capital cushions alongside risk weights.
  • Preserve innovation while assessing specific market failures; policy preferences are not outcome forecasts.

Tools and charts discussed

Mentioned in the transcript; visual charts have not all been inspected.

  • Historical world GDP per person chart is described but not reconstructed.
  • GDP expenditure identity and net-export arithmetic.
  • Bank leverage and equity-loss buffers.
